newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says France, Germany do not want weak euro.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says France, Germany do not want weak euro.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, dismissing speculation that entry criteria for the planned single European currency would be diluted, said on Monday neither France nor Germany wanted a weak euro currency.
"Neither France nor Germany want a weak currency," Kohl told a news conference in response to a question after French and German leaders met ahead of a weekend European Union summit in Dublin.
Kohl told reporters it made no sense to speculate on which nations would be initial members of the currency union, which is due to start in January 1999 as detailed in the Maastricht Treaty.

But Kohl said EU finance ministers were still preparing for stability pact talks in Dublin. A source at the Nuremberg summit said Germany and France made little progress in resolving their differences over the pact that Germany has pushed to ensure fiscal discipline within monetary union.

Germany has found itself at odds with France -- and most of the rest of the EU -- in trying to set up a very strict budget pact which will mean semi-automatic penalties for countries whose governments overspend.
Kohl also said talks were going on over technicalities about the so-called EMS II system which will seek to group into a loose confederation nations that do not initially join the new currency union.
